title: Parameterization
body:
Describing a curve or a surface as the image of a function of one or two parameters, so that an
integral over it becomes an ordinary integral over the parameters. Every integral in
[[Vector Calculus]] is evaluated this way: **parameterise, substitute, integrate over the
parameter domain.**

## Curves: one parameter

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t),\, z(t) \rangle, \qquad a \le t \le b
$$

This is [[Parametric Equations]] from [[CALCULUS 2]] with a third component. The derivative
$\mathbf{r}'(t)$ is the velocity, tangent to the curve, and

$$
ds = \|\mathbf{r}'(t)\|\,dt, \qquad d\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt
$$

are the two elements a [[Line Integral]] needs: $ds$ (a scalar length, the same $ds$ as
[[Arc Length]]) and $d\mathbf{r}$ (a vector displacement). Standard parameterisations worth
knowing without deriving:

| Curve | Parameterisation |
|---|---|
| Line from $A$ to $B$ | $\mathbf{r}(t) = A + t(B-A)$, $0 \le t \le 1$ |
| Circle radius $a$ | $\langle a\cos t, a\sin t\rangle$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$ |
| Graph $y = f(x)$ | $\langle t, f(t)\rangle$ |

**Orientation is part of the data.** Reversing $t$ flips the sign of $\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}$
but leaves $\int_C f\,ds$ alone, because the vector element carries a direction and the length
element does not.

## Surfaces: two parameters

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \langle x(u,v),\, y(u,v),\, z(u,v) \rangle
$$

Two parameters sweep out a two-dimensional sheet. The two [[Partial Derivative|partials]]
$\mathbf{r}_u$ and $\mathbf{r}_v$ are tangent to the surface, so their cross product is **normal**
to it, and its length is the area distortion:

$$
d\mathbf{S} = (\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v)\,du\,dv, \qquad dS = \|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\|\,du\,dv
$$

Which is exactly the curve story one dimension up. The sphere of radius $a$ parameterises by
spherical angles as $\langle a\sin\phi\cos\theta, a\sin\phi\sin\theta, a\cos\phi\rangle$, giving
the familiar $dS = a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta$.

## The same idea as a change of variables

Choosing polar, cylindrical, or spherical coordinates in [[Multiple Integration]] is
parameterisation with the parameters being the new coordinates, and the Jacobian there plays the
role $\|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\|$ plays here. Both answer one question: **how much does
the parameter domain get stretched when it is mapped onto the thing you are integrating over.**
See [[Polar Coordinates]] for the two-dimensional case that starts it.
